metadata.title: Professional learning communities and teacher outcomes. A cross-national analysis

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher-level data collected via a two-stage probability sampling design (teachers randomly selected within randomly selected schools, with optional stratification within countries/economies). Analyses are conducted at the teacher level and incorporate TALIS 2018 sampling weights to account for unequal selection probabilities within each country/economy. For the pooled cross-national analysis, the authors rescale the official teacher weights and replicate weights into senate weights so that each country has equal influence on the pooled estimates. The manuscript does not report a single named weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that weights and replicate weights are used in the R 'survey' package framework; therefore, results are intended to be population-representative within each participating country/economy.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variables are TALIS teacher scales (job satisfaction, self-efficacy, and clarity of instruction) rather than cognitive achievement scores that TALIS/PISA-style PVs are designed to represent. The paper instead uses scale scores derived from TALIS questionnaires and compares associations across countries using survey-weighted generalized linear models. Missing data handling is addressed via multiple imputation as a robustness check, so PV-specific missingness strategies are not relevant here.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses TALIS 2018 ISCED level 2 teacher data. For cross-national comparability in the pooled analysis, countries with missing data on any key PLC variables or teacher outcome/control variables were excluded: Estonia, France, Hungary, Mexico, and Saudi Arabia were excluded because PLC scale data were missing; Russia was excluded from the pooled analysis because self-efficacy data were missing; and Spain was excluded because teachers’ level of education was missing. The final pooled dataset includes 127,339 teachers from 40 countries, with an average of 188 schools per country and 17 teachers per school. All continuous variables (PLC constructs and teacher outcomes) were standardized to mean 0 and SD 1. The authors also report that they replicated pooled results using multiple imputation of missing data as a robustness check (Appendix C), and that country-level analyses exclude Russia due to missing self-efficacy.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 ISCED level 2 (teacher-level) — job satisfaction with work environment (T3JSENV)
top_predictors: Collaborative practice with focus on student learning (CPL)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pooled analysis (survey-weighted GLM): PLC coefficient = 0.197 SD; PLC→job satisfaction stronger than PLC→self-efficacy (0.059–0.062 SD) and PLC→clarity of instruction (0.041–0.048 SD). Subdimensions: SVR = 0.248 SD; SC = 0.131 SD; CPL = 0.076 SD. Country-level: PLC→job satisfaction positive and significant in all countries except Cyprus; magnitudes mostly 0.150–0.351 SD.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 ISCED level 2 teacher the study leveraged Professional learning community (PLC) and its subdimensions (especially Shared vision and responsibilities) to predict teacher job satisfaction (T3JSENV), finding that PLC was positively and statistically significantly associated with job satisfaction (0.197 SD), with the strongest contribution from SVR (0.248 SD). This indicates that policies and school-level interventions that build shared vision, collective responsibility, and supportive conditions for PLCs may improve teacher morale and retention-relevant outcomes, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 ISCED level 2 (teacher-level) — self-efficacy in instruction (T3SEINS)
top_predictors: Collaborative practice with focus on student learning (CPL)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pooled analysis (survey-weighted GLM): PLC coefficient = 0.059–0.062 SD; SVR and SC show weaker associations than job satisfaction (SC reported 0.022–0.131 SD; CPL reported 0.076 SD for PLC subdimension effects overall). Country-level: PLC→self-efficacy positive and significant in 27 of 40 countries; magnitudes mostly 0.05–0.10 SD, with stronger cases Georgia (0.166 SD), Shanghai (China) (0.163 SD), and Vietnam (0.186 SD).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 ISCED level 2 teacher the study leveraged Professional learning community (PLC) and its subdimensions to predict teacher self-efficacy (T3SEINS), finding that PLC had a weak but positive association in the pooled analysis (about 0.059–0.062 SD) and was statistically significant in 27 of 40 countries with magnitudes typically 0.05–0.10 SD. This indicates that PLCs may support teachers’ instructional confidence only under certain contextual conditions, so implementation guidance should emphasize context fit rather than assuming uniform effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 ISCED level 2 (teacher-level) — clarity of instruction (T3CLAIN)
top_predictors: Collaborative practice with focus on student learning (CPL)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pooled analysis (survey-weighted GLM): PLC coefficient = 0.041–0.048 SD; SC reported weak relationships (0.022–0.131 SD). Country-level: PLC→clarity of instruction significant in about half of countries (21 of 40) with magnitudes generally around 0.1 SD; notable stronger cases Georgia (0.163 SD), Kazakhstan (0.141 SD), and Shanghai (China) (0.126 SD). CPL→clarity of instruction strongest in Alberta (Canada), Israel, Shanghai (China), and the United States with magnitudes 0.137–0.194 SD.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 ISCED level 2 teacher the study leveraged Professional learning community (PLC) and its subdimensions to predict clarity of instruction (T3CLAIN), finding that the pooled association was small (0.041–0.048 SD) and often statistically insignificant across countries (significant in 21 of 40). This indicates that PLCs may only modestly translate into perceived instructional clarity, suggesting that PLC designs should include concrete, instruction-focused collaboration mechanisms (e.g., CPL-like practices) and be evaluated for context-dependent effectiveness.

data.outcome_summary: This cross-national study uses TALIS 2018 teacher data for ISCED level 2 to examine whether engagement in professional learning communities (PLCs) is associated with teacher job satisfaction, self-efficacy in instruction, and clarity of instruction. The authors construct a school-level PLC measure as a shared cluster construct with three subdimensions (CPL, SVR, SC) and estimate survey-weighted generalized linear models at the teacher level, using TALIS sampling weights and replicate weights (rescaled to senate weights for pooled estimates). In the pooled analysis across 40 countries/economies, PLCs show the strongest relationship with job satisfaction (0.197 SD; SVR = 0.248 SD), while associations with self-efficacy (0.059–0.062 SD) and clarity of instruction (0.041–0.048 SD) are weak. Country results show substantial heterogeneity: PLCs predict job satisfaction in nearly all countries except Cyprus, but self-efficacy and clarity are significant in only subsets of countries. The study is cross-sectional, relies on teacher self-reports (especially for clarity), and uses multiple imputation as a robustness check; therefore, causal effects cannot be inferred.
